extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners in chemistry and pharmacy laboratories
extracted.subtask_description: Practical laboratory procedures and quality rules for separating mixtures (siphons, filtration, decantation, evaporation, crystallization, distillation) aimed at accurate preparative and analytical work in chemical and pharmaceutical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Siphon operation (priming and use)
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a siphon work the air contained in its interior must be expelled; a small tube HI soldered to the branch BC serves for this. To start the siphon, close the extremity C with a finger and suck until all air is removed and the tube is filled with liquid; then remove the finger and the liquid will flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical notes: the siphon end A must be immersed to the desired depth in the source liquid; the siphon may be passed through a hole in a small board so it need not be held by hand. Use the small vent/tube HI to remove air. If the deposit and liquid approach equilibrium where slightest motion remixes them, use a siphon instead of simple decantation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter concept and material selection
rubrics_metrics.description: A filter is a very fine and tight sieve through which solid particles, however divided, cannot pass while fluids do; in pharmacy thick woollen cloths and very close-woven fabric (woollen with nap) are particularly suitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form conical filters (chausse) so all liquid collects at a single point for easy reception. Use wooden chassis for larger filters. Match filter material to experiment: cloth for some operations, paper for general use when many different experiments make reuse of cloth impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of paper as filter and necessary supports
rubrics_metrics.description: Unstarched paper, though thin, is felted and tight enough to retain any solid particles while letting fluids pass; however it tears and punctures easily when wet and tends to adhere to glass funnels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support paper with doublings or various linings (toiles) and use a chassis with iron points or crochets for larger quantities. To prevent adhesion to glass and improve flow, pleat the paper or use spacers (straw fragments) or, preferably, small curved glass strips (6–8) hooked to the funnel rim to keep the paper away from the walls so liquid runs along the strips to the cone point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folding and pleating filters to avoid slow flow
rubrics_metrics.description: When paper is placed in a glass funnel it can press against the walls and only the cone tip filters, making filtration very slow and prone to obstruction by heavier heterogeneous particles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies include multiplying folds (pleating) so liquid follows the furrows, inserting straw fragments before placing paper, or using curved glass strips to maintain a gap—these allow the liquid to flow along channels to the cone point and prevent obstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and arrangement for multiple simultaneous filtrations
rubrics_metrics.description: For many concurrent filtrations it is convenient to have a board pierced with holes supported by uprights of wood to hold multiple funnels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a planche (board) AB with uprights AC, BD and holes to place funnels; this facilitates running many filtrations at once and organizing the setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-treatment of very viscous or thick liquids before filtration
rubrics_metrics.description: Very thick and viscous materials that cannot pass through paper filters can be treated to coagulate or remove viscous matter before filtering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common treatments: beat egg-white into such liquors and heat to coagulate the albumen which carries with it viscous matter (used for clarifying whey); for spirituous liquors a little dissolved fish glue coagulates under alcohol without heating. These steps improve filtrability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter chemical resistance—handling corrosive liquids
rubrics_metrics.description: A necessary condition for filtration is that the filter not be attacked or corroded by the liquid; thus concentrated acids cannot be filtered through paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use broken glass, pieces of quartz or rock crystal (coarse and partly powdered) placed in the funnel with larger fragments at the bottom and finer on top when filtering corrosive fluids like concentrated acids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sand filtration for clearing river water
rubrics_metrics.description: River sand is used to filter water for public use because its rounded fragments and a mixture of particle sizes favor water passage while preventing large voids and because well-rolled-and-washed sand contributes no soluble substances to the water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: rounded grains, graded sizes fill interstices, inert due to natural washing. Maintenance: sand filters must be washed in successive waters until the effluent is clear; cleaning is simple compared to other filters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleaning and maintenance of reusable filter media
rubrics_metrics.description: Filters used repeatedly will clog and cease to pass liquid if not cleaned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sand filters, wash in several successive waters until clear. For toile/fabric supports, wash or replace if impregnated with substances that could contaminate subsequent experiments. Replace paper filters between uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decantation procedure and suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Decantation separates concreted particles from a liquid by allowing the mixture to rest in conical vessels until the solid deposits and then pouring off the clear liquid; this presupposes the suspended body is specifically heavier than the liquid and will collect at the bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conical vessels (like drinking-glass-shaped vases). Pour gently by inclining to avoid remixing. If deposit has nearly same specific gravity as liquid so slight motion remixes it, use a siphon instead. For precise weighing of precipitates prefer decantation to filtration but wash precipitate thoroughly by repeated washings to remove soluble residues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer decantation for precise precipitate weighing
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining precisely the weight of a precipitate, decantation is preferable to filtration, provided the precipitate is carefully washed with large volumes of water several times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filtration can mislead when small quantities are involved because variability in filter dryness and retained moisture introduces error; decantation with thorough washing avoids these sources of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mechanical division from chemical division
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical division reduces a solid mass into many smaller masses by physical forces but cannot reach the elementary molecules; chemical agents divide matter down to molecular constituents without decomposing the molecules themselves (in the sense of the salt remaining a salt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mechanical means where coarse division suffices; use chemical agents when division to molecular scale is required (e.g., solutions). Recognize the limits of mechanical reduction compared to chemical action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solution of salts vs dissolution of metals (conceptual distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solution of salts in a fluid like water involves merely separating salt molecules without decomposition; dissolution of metals generally involves chemical decomposition of the acid or water (e.g., oxidation forming oxide and gas evolution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'solution' and 'dissolution' differently in analysis and experiment. When working with salts, expect recoverability of both salt and solvent in original amounts; with metal dissolution expect chemical change and gas evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of caloric (heat) vs water in salt solubility
rubrics_metrics.description: Solution of salts typically involves two effects: solution by water and solution by caloric (heat). The solubility at hot vs cold depends on how fusible the salt is by caloric alone—salts easily liquefied by heat tend to be much more soluble in hot water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To predict or interpret solubility behavior, consider the salt's melting point (fusibility) and measure solubility at different temperatures. If a salt is little soluble in water but melts at moderately low heat, expect greater solubility in hot water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method for characterizing salt solubility
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine for each salt the quantity that dissolves in a given amount of water at different thermometer degrees, and relate this to known caloric content per degree to find the proportions of caloric and water required to hold the salt in solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematic experiments at various temperatures; measure what caloric is absorbed when the salt liquefies and what is released at crystallization. This empirical approach completes the theoretical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus recommendations for solutions and evaporations
rubrics_metrics.description: For small operations use medicine phials, terrines of gres, matras with elongated necks, copper or silver casseroles/basins; for evaporation capsules, thin glass (fragments of retorts, medicine vials) and porcelain jats or terrines are useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thin, uniformly thin glass pieces (e.g., bottoms of cornues or portions of matras) are best for capsules because their even thinness tolerates sudden heating and cooling. For many simultaneous evaporations use small medicine vials placed on a second grill over a gentle fire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaporation practice: air vs caloric-driven processes
rubrics_metrics.description: There is slow evaporation at air-exposed surfaces (partly by air and partly by caloric, accompanied by cooling) and vaporization of a continuously boiling fluid chiefly driven by caloric; the latter depends on caloric supplied, not surface area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covering an actively boiling evaporating vessel to some extent is acceptable if the cover is a poor conductor of heat, since trapped caloric aids vaporization. Strong cold air currents can remove caloric and slow evaporation. For valuable volatile components, prefer distillation rather than evaporation which sacrifices the volatile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaporation apparatus and heating methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Use copper/silver basins, casseroles, lead vessels, glass capsules, porcelain, or thin glass flasks; cornues may be placed on sand baths or inside reverberatory furnaces depending on method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sand baths are slower and risk breaking glass due to unequal heating; when intense fire is required use crucibles of earth. Thin glass vessels (fioles à médecine) are economical and tolerate fire well. To cut glass vessels for making capsules, heat with iron rings and quench to fracture along the heated circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallization control by cooling rate and rest
rubrics_metrics.description: If cooling is slow and the liquid is at rest, molecules arrange regularly and give proper crystallization; if cooling is rapid or the liquid is agitated during solidification, crystallization is confused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for slow evaporation/cooling in a tranquil place to obtain larger and more regular crystals. Use elevated vessels with considerable liquid thickness for slow-air crystallization to get large crystals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallization of salts requiring removal of both water and caloric
rubrics_metrics.description: For salts that are easily liquefied by caloric it is not sufficient to remove the water; it is necessary also to remove caloric (heat) for crystallization to occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize salts (e.g., saltpeter, muriate oxygéné de potasse) that require both cooling and water removal. Practical refinement: dissolve mixed salts in hot water (enough to hold the least soluble in solution), cool to precipitate the more temperature-sensitive salt, and repeat dissolution/crystallization cycles to purify (as in saltpeter refining).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractional crystallization as a separation method
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate mixed salts by exploiting differences of solubility at hot and cold—dissolve in suitable quantity of hot water then cool to precipitate the less soluble salt and repeat to improve purity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study each component's solubility at given temperatures and consider solubility in alcohol or alcohol-water mixtures to increase separation options. Complete separation is difficult and may require multiple cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vessels recommended for crystallization
rubrics_metrics.description: Use terrines of gres and large flattened capsules; for slow evaporation at air and atmospheric heat use somewhat elevated vessels to afford a thicker layer of liquid and thus produce larger crystals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select vessel geometry according to desired crystal size: deeper vessels favor larger crystals; wide shallow vessels favor many small crystals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distillation simple—purpose and apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple distillation separates two bodies when one is more volatile by converting the more volatile to gas and condensing it; it is essentially an evaporation in closed vessels aimed at collecting the volatile product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic apparatus: a distilling bottle or 'cornue' with curved neck, cucurbite with chapiteau, alambic with tubulure (which may be stopped with a crystal plug). The chapiteau should have a gutter to collect condensate and a beak to pour it out. For pharmacy operations glass cucurbites and single-piece glass alembics are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety in distillation—venting expansion of vapors
rubrics_metrics.description: Because distillation involves expansion of vapors that could burst vessels, a small hole T must be provided in the receiver or vessel to give vapors an outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always provide ventilation/vent hole in the collecting vessel to avoid pressure buildup. Lute joints appropriately but ensure a safe pressure relief path (small hole) when necessary to prevent explosion.
